levels.title: First Steps
levels.blurb: Find your way around the terminal and make your very first Git commit.

levels.title: Snapshots
levels.blurb: Read your history, compare changes, and keep junk out of your repo.

levels.title: Branching Out
levels.blurb: Create branches, merge them back, and calmly handle your first conflicts.

levels.title: Teamwork
levels.blurb: Share code with remotes, open pull requests, and install your first npm packages.

levels.title: Pro Habits
levels.blurb: Undo safely, manage dependencies, guard your secrets, and let tools tidy your code.

questions.prompt: What does the `pwd` command do in the terminal?
choices: Prints the full path of the folder you are in
Lists every file and folder inside the current folder
Moves you back to the folder you were in before
Creates a new password for your user account
questions.hint: The letters stand for three words about where you are.
questions.explain: `pwd` means "print working directory". It shows the full path of the folder your terminal is in right now, which is handy when you feel lost.

questions.prompt: Which command produced this output?
choices: `pwd`
`ls`
`mkdir`
`clear`
questions.hint: You wanted to see what is inside the current folder.
questions.explain: `ls` lists the files and folders in the current directory. Here it shows two files and a `scripts` folder.

questions.prompt: What does `mkdir portfolio` do?
choices: Creates an empty file named `portfolio`
Creates a new folder named `portfolio`
Opens the folder named `portfolio`
Deletes the folder named `portfolio`
questions.hint: Think of it as "make directory".
questions.explain: `mkdir` is short for "make directory". It creates a new, empty folder.

questions.prompt: Which of these commands only show information and do not change anything? Select all that apply.
choices: `pwd`
`ls -a`
`ls`
`mkdir notes`
questions.hint: One of them makes something new.
questions.explain: `pwd`, `ls`, and `ls -a` only report information, so they are always safe to run. `mkdir notes` creates a new folder.

questions.prompt: Type the terminal command that moves you into a folder named `blog` inside your current folder.
questions.hint: The command is two letters long, and the folder name goes after it.
questions.explain: `cd blog` changes your current folder to `blog`. Run `pwd` afterwards if you want to check where you are.

questions.prompt: Why does `.git` appear only in the second listing?
choices: The first `ls` could not read the folder, so it showed less
`.git` was created by another program between the two commands
`-a` also shows hidden items whose names start with a dot
`-a` creates a `.git` folder first and then lists everything
questions.hint: Look at the first character of the extra names.
questions.explain: Names that start with a dot are hidden by default. `ls -a` shows all entries, including hidden ones like `.git`.

questions.prompt: What is version control?
choices: A system that records changes to your files so you can go back
A setting that decides which browser version can open your site
A program that compresses your project so it loads faster
A tool that checks your code for spelling and grammar mistakes
questions.hint: Think "save points" for a whole project.
questions.explain: Version control keeps a history of changes. You can see who changed what and when, and go back to an earlier version if something breaks.

questions.prompt: If you delete the `.git` folder, you lose the Git history of that project.
questions.hint: Think about where Git keeps every commit.
questions.explain: All history lives inside `.git`. Your current files stay, but the commits are gone unless a copy exists somewhere else, like on GitHub.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?
choices: Git is a website; GitHub is the program you install on your computer
Git works only with JavaScript; GitHub works with every language
They are two names for the same program from the same company
Git tracks history on your computer; GitHub hosts repositories online
questions.hint: One of them works fine without the internet.
questions.explain: Git runs on your computer and tracks history. GitHub is an online service where you can store Git repositories and collaborate with others.

questions.prompt: You are in `/Users/sam/projects/blog`. Which folder are you in after running this command?
choices: `/Users/sam`
`/Users/sam/projects`
`/Users/sam/projects/blog/..`
questions.hint: Two dots mean "the parent of where I am".
questions.explain: `..` refers to the parent folder, so `cd ..` moves you up exactly one level, from `blog` to `projects`.

questions.prompt: What does `git init` do?
questions.code:
$ cd my-site
$ git init
Initialized empty Git repository in /Users/sam/my-site/.git/
choices: Installs Git on your computer for the first time
Makes the current folder a Git repository
Downloads a copy of a project from GitHub
Saves all current changes as the first commit
questions.hint: It is how a brand-new project starts using Git.
questions.explain: `git init` creates a hidden `.git` folder where Git stores all history. Your files stay as they are; Git just starts watching the folder.

questions.prompt: What does this command set?
choices: Your GitHub login username and password
The name of your main branch
The author name recorded on your commits
The name of the folder for the current repository
questions.hint: Every commit remembers who made it.
questions.explain: Git stores an author name and email on each commit. `--global` sets the name for every repository on your computer.

questions.prompt: What does `git add index.html` do?
choices: Uploads `index.html` to your repository on GitHub
Stages the changes in `index.html` for the next commit
Saves `index.html` in a new commit right away, with no message
Creates a new empty file called `index.html`
questions.hint: It is the step before committing.
questions.explain: `git add` stages changes. Staged changes are what the next `git commit` will save.

questions.prompt: One commit can include changes to several files at once.
questions.hint: Think about what you can put in the staging area.
questions.explain: A commit saves everything you staged, whether that is one file or many. It is a good idea to group related changes in one commit.

questions.prompt: Which of these are benefits of using version control? Select all that apply.
choices: You can see what changed and when
Several people can work on one project
Your website loads faster for visitors
You can go back to an earlier version
questions.hint: Version control is about history and teamwork, not speed.
questions.explain: Version control tracks history, lets you restore old versions, and helps teams work together. It does not change how fast your site runs.

questions.prompt: Type the full Git command (starting with `git`) that shows which files are changed, staged, or untracked.
questions.hint: Its output starts with a line like `On branch main`.
questions.explain: `git status` is your best friend. Run it often to see what Git thinks is going on.

questions.prompt: What is a commit in Git?
choices: A promise to finish a feature at a later time
A copy of your project uploaded to the internet
A saved snapshot of your staged changes
A list of the files that Git should ignore
questions.hint: It is the "save point" in your history.
questions.explain: A commit records a snapshot of the staged changes. Each commit has a message, an author, a date, and a unique ID called a hash.

questions.prompt: You need an internet connection to make a Git commit.
questions.hint: Where does the `.git` folder live?
questions.explain: Git works locally. Commits are saved in the `.git` folder on your computer. You only need the internet to share them, for example with `git push`.

questions.prompt: In this command, what is the `-m` option for?
choices: It moves the commit to another folder
It gives the commit its message
It marks the commit as the most important one
It merges the commit into `main`
questions.hint: The text in quotes is the clue.
questions.explain: `-m` lets you write the commit message right in the command. Without it, Git opens a text editor so you can type the message there.

questions.prompt: What does "Untracked files" mean in this output?
questions.code:
$ git status
On branch main

No commits yet

Untracked files:
  (use "git add <file>..." to include in what will be committed)
	index.html
choices: `index.html` was saved in a commit but then changed
Git cannot open `index.html` because of a permission problem
`index.html` was deleted from the folder but Git remembers it
Git sees `index.html` but is not tracking it yet
questions.hint: Read the helpful line in brackets.
questions.explain: An untracked file is new to Git. It is in the folder, but it is not part of any commit yet. `git add index.html` starts tracking it.

questions.prompt: What does `git add .` stage?
choices: Only files that Git already tracks, and no new files at all
Only files whose names start with a dot
Only the file you edited most recently
All changes in the current folder and its subfolders
questions.hint: In the terminal, a single dot means "this folder".
questions.explain: The dot means the current directory. `git add .` stages every new, changed, or deleted file inside it, so check `git status` first.

questions.prompt: Why does Git have a staging area between editing files and committing?
choices: So other people can edit the same files at the same time as you
So Git can back up your files to the cloud before each commit
So you can choose exactly which changes go into the next commit
So your files open faster when you switch between editors
questions.hint: Imagine you changed three files but only want to save two.
questions.explain: The staging area lets you build each commit on purpose. You can stage some changes now and leave others for a later commit.

questions.prompt: You edited `app.js` in an existing repository and want to save it in history. Which two commands do you run? Select all that apply.
questions.code:
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   app.js
choices: `git push`
`git add app.js`
`git commit -m "Update app"`
`git save app.js`
questions.hint: Stage first, then save.
questions.explain: First stage the change with `git add`, then save it with `git commit`. `git push` only shares commits that already exist, and `git save` is not a Git command.

questions.prompt: Complete the command that sets the email recorded on your commits: `git config --global user.____ "sam@example.com"`. Type only the missing word.
questions.hint: Each commit stores a name and one more way to contact the author.
questions.explain: `user.email` sets the email on your commits, next to `user.name`. GitHub uses this email to link your commits to your account.

questions.prompt: What does `git log` show?
choices: Files that are not committed yet
The list of commits, newest first
Errors from your last build
Every command you typed in the terminal
questions.hint: It is the project's diary.
questions.explain: `git log` shows commit history with hashes, authors, dates, and messages. The newest commit is at the top.

questions.prompt: What does the `--oneline` option change here?
questions.code:
$ git log --oneline
3f9c2ab Add contact form
91d04e7 Style the header
c2a7710 Initial commit
choices: Each commit fits on one short line
Only the single newest commit is shown
Only commits made today are shown
All commits are combined into one
questions.hint: Compare it with the long, multi-line normal output.
questions.explain: `--oneline` gives a compact view: one line per commit. It is great for a quick look at history.

questions.prompt: In `git log --oneline` output, what is `3f9c2ab`?
choices: The name of the branch it is on
The date the commit was made
A short form of the commit's ID
The number of lines that changed
questions.hint: Git uses it to point at one exact commit.
questions.explain: Each commit has a unique hash. Git shows a short prefix of it, and you can use it in commands like `git show 3f9c2ab`.

questions.prompt: You ran `git log` and the output fills the screen with a `:` at the bottom. How do you get back to your prompt?
questions.code:
commit 3f9c2ab41e0d7c5b8a2f6e19d0c4b7a8e5f3d2c1
Author: Sam <sam@example.com>
Date:   Mon Oct 26 10:12:44 2026

    Add contact form
:
choices: Press `q`
Type `exit` and press Enter
Close the terminal window
Press Enter until it ends
questions.hint: The pager waits for a single key, not a typed command.
questions.explain: Long output opens in a pager. Press `q` to quit it. You can scroll with the arrow keys first if you like.

questions.prompt: You see this status. What will plain `git diff` show you?
questions.code:
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   style.css
choices: The exact lines you changed in `style.css`
The commit that last changed `style.css`
Nothing, because `git diff` only shows commits
A list of all commits that touched `style.css`
questions.hint: Diff means difference, line by line.
questions.explain: `git diff` compares your working files with the staging area, so it shows unstaged edits line by line.

questions.prompt: Which of these can `git status` tell you? Select all that apply.
choices: Which branch you are on
Which files have staged changes
Which files are untracked
Who wrote each line of a file
questions.hint: It reports the current state of your work, not the history.
questions.explain: `git status` shows your branch and which files are staged, changed, or untracked. It does not show who wrote each line; other commands do that.

questions.prompt: Git tracks empty folders, so a new empty folder appears in `git status`.
questions.hint: Git cares about the contents of files.
questions.explain: Git tracks files, not folders. An empty folder will not show up until it contains at least one file.

questions.prompt: Complete the command to see your staged changes: `git diff --____`. Type only the missing word.
questions.hint: Think of the area you put changes in with `git add`.
questions.explain: `git diff --staged` (also written `--cached`) shows what will go into your next commit.

questions.prompt: Which commit message is the most helpful?
choices: Fix typo in signup form label
more work on the stuff from yesterday
Updated a bunch of files and fixed some things
update
questions.hint: Would a teammate understand it in six months?
questions.explain: A good message says what the commit does in a short, specific summary. "Fix typo in signup form label" tells you exactly what changed.

questions.prompt: Which habit makes your history easiest to understand?
choices: Small commits that each hold one logical change
A commit after every single keystroke
One big commit at the end of each week
Committing only when the whole project is finished
questions.hint: Think about finding one change later.
questions.explain: Small, focused commits are easy to read, review, and undo. Each one tells a clear part of the story.

questions.prompt: What is a `.gitignore` file for?
choices: Storing commit messages you want to reuse later
Hiding your repository from other people on GitHub
Listing commits that Git should hide in the `git log` output
Listing files and folders that Git should not track
questions.hint: Some files should never end up in a commit.
questions.explain: `.gitignore` tells Git which files to leave out, such as build output, logs, or dependency folders.

questions.prompt: With this `.gitignore`, which file will Git ignore?
choices: `logo.png`
`debug.log`
`log.js`
`changelog.md`
questions.hint: `*` matches any name; look at what must come after it.
questions.explain: `*.log` matches any name that ends in `.log`. Only `debug.log` ends that way.

questions.prompt: What does the line `dist/` in `.gitignore` do?
choices: Ignores the `dist` folder and everything inside it
Ignores only files named `dist`, not folders
Deletes the `dist` folder the next time you commit
Tells Git to track only the `dist` folder and nothing else
questions.hint: The trailing slash means "a folder".
questions.explain: A pattern ending in `/` matches a directory. Everything inside an ignored folder is ignored too.

questions.prompt: In a typical JavaScript project, which of these usually belong in `.gitignore`? Select all that apply.
choices: `index.html`
`.env`
`.DS_Store`
`node_modules/`
questions.hint: Ignore things that are generated, secret, or system clutter.
questions.explain: `node_modules/` can be reinstalled, `.env` holds secrets, and `.DS_Store` is a macOS system file. `index.html` is real source code, so you commit it.

questions.prompt: Adding a file that is already committed to `.gitignore` makes Git stop tracking it automatically.
questions.hint: What does Git do with files it already tracks?
questions.explain: `.gitignore` only affects untracked files. To stop tracking a committed file, run `git rm --cached <file>` and then commit.

questions.prompt: In a `.gitignore` file, which character starts a comment line? Type the single character.
questions.hint: Many config files use this same symbol for comments.
questions.explain: Lines starting with `#` are comments. Git skips them, so you can explain your rules.

questions.prompt: In this diff, what does the line starting with `+` mean?
choices: The line was added
The line was removed
The line is unchanged
The line has an error
questions.hint: Plus and minus mean what they usually mean.
questions.explain: In a diff, `-` lines were removed and `+` lines were added. Here `red` was replaced with `blue`.

questions.prompt: What does `git show 3f9c2ab` do?
choices: Moves your files back to that commit and keeps them there
Shows the files that were untracked at that time
Shows that commit's message and the changes it made
Removes that commit from the history of the branch
questions.hint: It only displays information.
questions.explain: `git show` prints the details of one commit: author, date, message, and its diff. It changes nothing.

questions.prompt: What does `git diff --staged` show?
choices: Changes in your files that you have not staged yet
Changes you staged, compared with the last commit
Files that Git ignores because of `.gitignore`
All differences between your two newest branches
questions.hint: It previews what your next commit will contain.
questions.explain: `git diff --staged` shows exactly what `git commit` would save right now. It is a great final check before committing.

questions.prompt: You ran `git add style.css`, then edited `style.css` again. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Plain `git diff` now shows your newest edits
The next commit saves only the staged version unless you run `git add` again
Plain `git diff` shows nothing because the file is already staged
Git stages your new edits for you automatically
questions.hint: `git add` takes a snapshot at the moment you run it.
questions.explain: Staging saves the file as it was when you ran `git add`. Your later edits are unstaged, so `git diff` shows them, and the commit leaves them out until you stage them too.

questions.prompt: You staged `notes.txt` by mistake. What does this command do?
choices: Unstages it and keeps your edits in the file
Throws away your edits to `notes.txt` for good
Deletes `notes.txt` from your computer and from Git
Commits `notes.txt` with an empty message
questions.hint: The `--staged` part only affects the staging area.
questions.explain: `git restore --staged` removes the file from the staging area. Your changes are still in the file, so nothing is lost.

questions.prompt: What does `git restore style.css` do when the file has unstaged edits?
questions.code:
$ git status
Changes not staged for commit:
	modified:   style.css
$ git restore style.css
choices: Throws those edits away and brings back the saved version
Moves those edits into the staging area for you
Creates a backup copy named `style.css.bak` and keeps both files
Saves those edits in a new commit on the branch
questions.hint: Use it when you want to throw away your experiment.
questions.explain: `git restore <file>` replaces your working copy with the version from the staging area (which matches the last commit if nothing is staged). The unstaged edits are gone, so use it with care. The older command was `git checkout -- <file>`.

questions.prompt: You can commit the `.gitignore` file so your whole team shares the same ignore rules.
questions.hint: It is just a normal text file in the project.
questions.explain: Committing `.gitignore` is common practice. Everyone who clones the project gets the same rules.

questions.prompt: Type the full Git command (starting with `git`, no options) that shows the commit history.
questions.hint: Think of a diary that lists every entry, newest first.
questions.explain: `git log` lists your commits, newest first. Add `--oneline` for a compact view.

questions.prompt: What is a branch in Git?
choices: A folder that holds older copies of your files
A separate line of work with its own commits
A list of the people allowed to commit to a project
A backup copy of the whole `.git` folder
questions.hint: Picture a road that splits.
questions.explain: A branch is a named pointer to a line of commits. You can build a feature on its own branch while `main` stays untouched.

questions.prompt: In this output, what does the `*` mean?
choices: `navbar` has changes that are not committed yet
`navbar` is the newest branch
`navbar` is the default branch
`navbar` is the branch you are on now
questions.hint: Git marks one branch specially.
questions.explain: `git branch` lists local branches and marks the current one with `*`.

questions.prompt: What does `git switch -c feature/login` do?
questions.code:
$ git switch -c feature/login
Switched to a new branch 'feature/login'
choices: Switches to `feature/login`, but only if it already exists
Copies the commits of `feature/login` into the current branch
Deletes the branch named `feature/login`
Creates a branch named `feature/login` and switches to it
questions.hint: Plain `git switch` needs a branch that already exists. What does the extra option add?
questions.explain: `git switch -c` creates a new branch and moves you onto it in one step.

questions.prompt: You are on `main` and run `git switch -c feature/login`. Where does the new branch start?
choices: At the commit that `main` points to right now
At the very first commit in the repository
At a new empty commit with no files in it
At the newest commit on GitHub's copy of `main`
questions.hint: Think about where you are standing when you create it.
questions.explain: A new branch starts at your current commit, so it already has all of `main`'s work. It does not start empty, and it does not look at GitHub.

questions.prompt: What does `git branch new-idea` do?
questions.code:
$ git branch new-idea
$ git branch
* main
  new-idea
choices: Creates `new-idea` and keeps you where you are
Switches to an existing branch called `new-idea`
Renames the current branch to `new-idea`
Creates `new-idea` and then moves you onto it right away
questions.hint: Check `git branch` afterwards: where is the `*`?
questions.explain: `git branch <name>` only creates the branch. You stay on your current branch until you switch to the new one.

questions.prompt: Creating a new branch copies all of your project files into a new folder.
questions.hint: Branches are very cheap to create.
questions.explain: A branch is just a small pointer to a commit. Your files stay in the same folder, and Git updates them when you switch.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Git branches are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each branch can have its own new commits
Switching branches updates the files in your folder
You must push a branch before you can commit on it
A repository can have only two branches at a time
questions.hint: A branch is a small pointer to commits on your computer.
questions.explain: Each branch moves ahead with its own commits, and switching updates your files to match. You can have many branches, and you can commit on them long before you push.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: `git ____ feature` brings the commits from `feature` into your current branch. Type only the missing word.
questions.hint: Two roads join into one.
questions.explain: `git merge feature` combines the work from `feature` into the branch you are on.

questions.prompt: Why might a developer create a branch for a new feature?
choices: To hide the feature's commits from the `git log` command
To make the feature run faster after it goes to production
To work on it without affecting the working code on `main`
Because Git allows only one commit on each branch
questions.hint: Think of a safe place to experiment.
questions.explain: Branches let you try ideas safely. If the feature works, you merge it. If not, you can just delete the branch.

questions.prompt: Which command moves you onto an existing branch called `main`?
choices: `git branch main`
`git switch main`
`git merge main`
`git init main`
questions.hint: You want to change which branch you are on.
questions.explain: `git switch main` makes `main` your current branch and updates your files to match it. The older form is `git checkout main`.

questions.prompt: What happens when you run these commands?
questions.code:
$ git switch main
$ git merge add-footer
choices: Both branches are deleted and replaced with a new one
The `add-footer` branch is renamed to `main`
The work from `main` is brought into `add-footer`
The work from `add-footer` is brought into `main`
questions.hint: You merge other work into the branch you are on.
questions.explain: `git merge <branch>` brings that branch's commits into your current branch. Here you are on `main`, so `main` gets the footer work.

questions.prompt: When Git reports a conflict, your repository is broken and you need to start over.
questions.hint: Git tells you exactly which files need your attention.
questions.explain: Conflicts are normal. Git simply asks you to decide which lines to keep. Edit the file, `git add` it, and commit.

questions.prompt: Your `add-footer` branch is merged into `main`. What does `git branch -d add-footer` do?
choices: Removes only the label; the commits stay in `main`
Undoes the merge, so `main` no longer has the footer work
Deletes the branch on GitHub, but keeps your local copy
Deletes every commit that was made on that branch
questions.hint: A branch is just a label pointing at commits.
questions.explain: Deleting a merged branch only removes the label. Its commits are already part of `main`, so nothing is lost.

questions.prompt: Why does Git refuse here?
questions.code:
$ git branch -d experiment
error: the branch 'experiment' is not fully merged
choices: You can only delete branches that a teammate created
`experiment` is checked out on a teammate's computer
Git never deletes a branch once it has been pushed
Its commits are not merged into your current branch yet
questions.hint: Git is protecting something.
questions.explain: `-d` only deletes a branch when its commits are already merged, so no work is lost. If you really want to throw the work away, `git branch -D` forces it, so be sure first.

questions.prompt: Which of these are valid Git branch names? Select all that apply.
choices: `feature/user-profile`
`my new branch`
`fix-login-redirect`
`fix..bug`
questions.hint: Git does not allow spaces or two dots in a row.
questions.explain: Dashes and slashes are fine and common. Spaces and `..` are not allowed in branch names.

questions.prompt: Older tutorials create and switch to a new branch with `git checkout __ navbar`. Type only the missing option.
questions.hint: It is one letter after a single dash.
questions.explain: `git checkout -b navbar` creates `navbar` and switches to it. Today, `git switch -c navbar` does the same job.

questions.prompt: What usually causes a merge conflict?
choices: A file name contains capital letters on one of the branches
One branch has many more commits than the other branch
Both branches changed the same lines differently
You merged the branches before pushing them to GitHub
questions.hint: Git cannot guess which edit you want.
questions.explain: Git merges different parts of a file on its own. When both sides edit the same lines, it asks you to choose.

questions.prompt: In this conflicted file, which version is between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`?
choices: The version from the branch you are merging in
The version from your current branch
The version from the very first commit
A version Git wrote by combining both sides
questions.hint: `HEAD` means "where I am right now".
questions.explain: The top part, after `<<<<<<< HEAD`, is your current branch. The part after `=======` comes from the branch you are merging (`greeting` here).

questions.prompt: During a conflict, the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` markers stay in the file until you remove them.
questions.hint: Git writes them into your file for you to see.
questions.explain: Git adds the markers to show both versions. You must delete them when you finish, or they end up in your code.

questions.prompt: You fixed the conflict in `index.html` and removed all markers. What should you do next?
questions.code:
$ git status
Unmerged paths:
  (use "git add <file>..." to mark resolution)
	both modified:   index.html
choices: Run `git init` to reset the repository
Run `git add index.html` and then `git commit`
Delete the branch you were merging, since it is done
Run `git merge` again so Git checks the file once more
questions.hint: Git tells you how to mark the file as resolved.
questions.explain: Staging the file tells Git the conflict is resolved. Then `git commit` finishes the merge.

questions.prompt: When resolving a conflict, which of these are valid choices? Select all that apply.
choices: Combine both versions by hand
Keep the incoming version of the lines
Commit the file with the markers still inside
Keep your version of the lines
questions.hint: You can pick any final content, as long as it is clean.
questions.explain: You decide the final content: yours, theirs, or a mix. Just remove the markers before you stage and commit.

questions.prompt: You are in the middle of a messy merge and want to go back to how things were before it. Which command does that?
questions.code:
$ git merge redesign
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in style.css
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
choices: `git merge --abort`
`git merge --stop`
`git switch main`
`git commit -m "Undo merge"`
questions.hint: You want to cancel the merge.
questions.explain: `git merge --abort` stops the merge and puts your branch back as it was before. `git merge --stop` is not a real option, and Git will not let you commit while conflicts remain.

questions.prompt: What does "Fast-forward" mean in this merge output?
questions.code:
$ git merge add-footer
Updating b2a0470..6952cca
Fast-forward
 footer.html | 12 ++++++++++++
choices: The merge happened only on the remote, not on your computer
Git merged the branches without checking the files for conflicts
Git skipped some of the commits so it could finish faster
Your branch had nothing new, so Git just moved it forward
questions.hint: Nothing new happened on your branch since the other one started.
questions.explain: If your branch has no commits the other branch lacks, Git can simply move your branch pointer forward. No merge commit is needed.

questions.prompt: Type the full Git command (starting with `git`) that lists your local branches.
questions.hint: Just the noun, no branch name.
questions.explain: `git branch` with no name lists local branches and marks the current one with `*`.

questions.prompt: What is a remote in Git?
choices: A named link to another copy of your repository
A tool for editing files on another computer over SSH
A branch that was deleted but can still be restored
A commit that is not finished and not pushed yet
questions.hint: It is somewhere else your code lives.
questions.explain: A remote is a nickname plus a URL for another copy of the repo. You push to it and pull from it to share work.

questions.prompt: What does `git push` do?
choices: Sends your local commits to the remote repository
Moves your uncommitted changes to another branch
Stages all changed files
Downloads new commits from the remote
questions.hint: You push things away from you.
questions.explain: `git push` uploads commits from your branch to its remote branch so others can see them.

questions.prompt: What does `git pull` do?
choices: Deletes local branches that no longer exist on the remote
Downloads new commits and combines them with your branch
Only downloads new commits and never changes your branch
Sends your local commits up to the remote
questions.hint: It is two steps in one.
questions.explain: `git pull` downloads new commits and then combines them with your current branch. If you and the remote both have new commits, Git may stop and ask you to choose merge or rebase first.

questions.prompt: What does this status line tell you?
questions.code:
$ git status
On branch main
Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits.
  (use "git push" to publish your local commits)
choices: You have 2 files that are not staged
You have 2 commits that are not on the remote yet
Two teammates are editing `main` right now
The remote has 2 new commits that you do not have yet
questions.hint: "Ahead" means you have something extra.
questions.explain: Your local `main` has 2 commits that `origin/main` does not have. Run `git push` to share them.

questions.prompt: You push a new branch for the first time. What does the `-u` option do?
choices: Undoes the last push you made to the remote repository
Remembers `origin/feature/search` as the upstream branch
Updates every branch on the remote at the same time
Uploads only the untracked files in your project folder
questions.hint: It links your local branch to the remote one.
questions.explain: `-u` (short for `--set-upstream`) connects your branch to its remote branch. After that, `git push` and `git pull` need no extra arguments.

questions.prompt: What do you get after running `git clone` on a GitHub repository? Select all that apply.
choices: Your GitHub password saved in the project
A new empty repository on your GitHub account
A remote that points back to the URL you cloned
A local copy of the project's full history
questions.hint: Cloning only sets things up on your own computer.
questions.explain: Cloning copies the full history and sets up a remote that points to the URL. It does not create anything on GitHub or save your password in the project.

questions.prompt: One local repository can have more than one remote.
questions.hint: Each remote is just a name plus a URL.
questions.explain: You can add as many remotes as you need with `git remote add`. For example, `origin` can be your fork and `upstream` the original project.

questions.prompt: Type the full Git command (starting with `git`) that downloads new commits from the remote without merging them.
questions.hint: It is the safe, look-first half of what `git pull` does.
questions.explain: `git fetch` downloads new commits and updates `origin/...` branches, leaving your own branch unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is a pull request (PR) on GitHub?
choices: A request to merge your branch, with space for review
A message asking the owner to give you write access
A command that downloads the newest code from GitHub
A list of every commit that is in the repository
questions.hint: You are asking others to accept your changes.
questions.explain: A PR shows your branch's changes, lets teammates review and comment, and is merged when everyone is happy.

questions.prompt: What makes a good pull request description?
choices: What changed, why it changed, and how to test it
A list of every command you typed while working on it
A copy of every file that was changed
Only the branch name, since the code speaks for itself
questions.hint: Help your reviewer understand quickly.
questions.explain: A clear description saves reviewers time. Explain the goal, the main changes, and how to check that it works.

questions.prompt: Which review comment is the most helpful and kind?
choices: Why would anyone write it like this? It makes no sense to me.
This naming is bad and confusing. Please fix all of it.
I would never do it this way, but it is your choice.
Could we rename `data` to `users`? The loop reads better.
questions.hint: Good feedback is specific and explains why.
questions.explain: Helpful comments suggest a concrete change and give the reason. Talking about the code, not the person, keeps reviews friendly.

questions.prompt: A reviewer asks for changes on your PR. What is a good response?
choices: Merge the PR anyway, because the code already works
Close the PR and open a new one with a different reviewer
Push fixes to the same branch and reply to the comments
Ignore the comments and wait for the reviewer to forget
questions.hint: Reviews are a conversation.
questions.explain: New commits on the same branch update the PR automatically. Replying to comments shows what you changed and keeps everyone in sync.

questions.prompt: After you open a pull request, pushing new commits to its branch adds them to the same PR.
questions.hint: Think about what a PR is connected to.
questions.explain: A PR tracks a branch, so new pushes show up in it right away. No need to open a new PR.

questions.prompt: Which of these are good pull request habits? Select all that apply.
choices: Review your own diff before asking others
Keep each PR focused on one change
Write a clear description of what and why
Mix several unrelated fixes into one PR
questions.hint: Make the reviewer's job easy.
questions.explain: Small, focused PRs with good descriptions are faster to review. Checking your own diff first often catches small mistakes.

questions.prompt: You cloned a project that has a `package.json`. What does running `npm install` with no package name do?
questions.code:
$ git clone https://github.com/user/shop.git
$ cd shop
$ npm install
choices: Creates a brand-new `package.json` with no dependencies
Publishes the project to the npm registry
Installs npm itself on your computer
Installs all the dependencies listed in `package.json`
questions.hint: It gets the project ready to run.
questions.explain: `npm install` reads `package.json` (and `package-lock.json`) and downloads every dependency into `node_modules`.

questions.prompt: What name does Git give by default to the remote you cloned from? Type just the name.
questions.hint: Run `git remote -v` right after a clone and read the first word.
questions.explain: After `git clone`, the source repository is saved as the remote `origin`.

questions.prompt: What does `git clone https://github.com/user/app.git` do?
choices: Uploads your current folder to GitHub as a new `app` repository
Downloads the project and its history into an `app` folder
Creates an empty repository named `app` on GitHub
Copies only the newest files into `app`, without history
questions.hint: It is how you get a project onto your computer.
questions.explain: `git clone` makes a full local copy: files, branches, and history. It also remembers where it came from as a remote.

questions.prompt: What does this output show?
questions.code:
$ git remote -v
origin  https://github.com/sam/blog.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/sam/blog.git (push)
choices: The last two commits that were pushed to GitHub
Two different repositories that you are working in
Your GitHub username and the password you saved
One remote, `origin`, and its fetch and push URLs
questions.hint: `-v` means verbose: show more detail.
questions.explain: `git remote -v` lists remotes with their URLs. Here, one remote called `origin` is used for both fetching and pushing.

questions.prompt: How is `git fetch` different from `git pull`?
choices: `fetch` uploads commits, while `pull` downloads them
`fetch` works only on the `main` branch, not on others
`fetch` deletes your local changes before it downloads
`fetch` downloads commits but leaves your branch alone
questions.hint: One of them is "look before you leap".
questions.explain: `git fetch` updates your copy of the remote branches, like `origin/main`, and leaves your work alone. You can then review and merge when ready.

questions.prompt: Your push was rejected. What is the usual fix?
questions.code:
$ git push
 ! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not
hint: have locally.
choices: Run `git pull` to get the new commits, then push again
Delete your local folder, clone it again, and redo your work
Wait a few minutes and run the same push again
Rename your branch and push it as a new one
questions.hint: Someone else pushed first.
questions.explain: The remote has commits you do not have yet. Pull them in (merge or rebase), fix any conflicts, and then your push will work. Never force-push a shared branch just to make the error go away.

questions.prompt: With this `package.json`, what does `npm run build` do?
choices: Opens `package.json` in your editor
Runs the `vite` command from the `dev` script
Downloads a package named `build` from npm
Runs `vite build` from the `build` script
questions.hint: Look at the value next to the `build` key.
questions.explain: `npm run <name>` runs the command stored under that name in `scripts`. Here `build` runs `vite build`, which makes a production build of your site.

questions.prompt: You can run the `test` script with `npm test`, without typing `run`.
questions.hint: Think about how common the `test` script is.
questions.explain: `npm test` and `npm start` are built-in shortcuts. Other scripts, like `dev` or `build`, need `npm run`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `package.json` are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It lists the packages the project depends on
It can define scripts like `dev` and `build`
It contains the downloaded code of every package
It should be listed in `.gitignore`
questions.hint: Think about what lives in `node_modules` instead.
questions.explain: `package.json` describes the project: its name, scripts, and dependencies. The package code lives in `node_modules`, and you do commit `package.json`.

questions.prompt: Complete the command to install the package `dayjs` and add it to your dependencies: `npm ____ dayjs`. Type only the missing word.
questions.hint: The same word you use to set up the whole project.
questions.explain: `npm install dayjs` (or the short `npm i dayjs`) downloads the package and records it in `dependencies` in `package.json`.

questions.prompt: You have half-finished changes and need to switch branches quickly. What does `git stash` do?
questions.code:
$ git status --short
 M header.js
$ git stash
$ git status --short
$
choices: Commits your changes on the current branch with an automatic message
Saves your changes aside and cleans your working folder
Pushes your changes to a hidden branch on the remote
Deletes your uncommitted changes forever, with no undo
questions.hint: Think of putting things in a drawer for later.
questions.explain: `git stash` stores your tracked changes in a stash and resets your files to the last commit. You can bring the changes back later.

questions.prompt: What does `git stash pop` do?
choices: Creates a new stash from your current uncommitted changes
Brings back the newest stash and removes it from the list
Deletes every stash in the list without applying them
Shows the list of stashes without changing any files
questions.hint: Think of taking the top plate off a stack.
questions.explain: `git stash pop` brings back your latest stashed changes and drops that stash. `git stash apply` does the same but keeps the stash.

questions.prompt: `git commit -am "Update"` also includes brand-new files that Git has never tracked.
questions.hint: Think about which files Git already knows about.
questions.explain: `-a` stages changes to tracked files only. New files still need `git add` first.

questions.prompt: You made a commit but have not pushed it. What does this command do?
choices: Moves the last commit onto a new branch called `HEAD~1`
Creates a new commit that reverses the last one
Deletes the last commit and all of its changes
Undoes the last commit but keeps its changes staged
questions.hint: `--soft` is the gentle option.
questions.explain: `HEAD~1` means one commit before the current one. `--soft` moves the branch back there but keeps your changes staged, so you can recommit them.

questions.prompt: You committed, then saw you forgot `footer.css`. The commit is not pushed yet. What do these commands do?
choices: Make a second commit that holds only `footer.css`
Add `footer.css` to every commit on the branch
Push the corrected commit to the remote repository straight away
Add `footer.css` to the last commit and keep its message
questions.hint: Amend means "change a little".
questions.explain: `--amend` replaces the last commit with one that also has your staged changes, and `--no-edit` keeps the old message. It rewrites the commit, so use it only on commits you have not pushed.

questions.prompt: Your last commit is local only and has a wrong message. Which of these could fix it? Select all that apply.
choices: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, then commit again
`git fetch`
`git commit --amend -m "Correct message"`
`git stash`
questions.hint: You need to change or redo the last commit.
questions.explain: `--amend` replaces the last commit directly. A soft reset undoes it while keeping the changes staged, so you can commit again with a new message.

questions.prompt: A commit that is already pushed and shared broke something. What is the safest way to undo it?
questions.code:
$ git log --oneline
7d1e0a4 Change checkout button
3f9c2ab Add contact form
choices: `git revert 7d1e0a4`
Edit the commit on GitHub to remove it
Delete the `.git` folder and clone again
`git reset --hard 3f9c2ab`, then force-push the branch
questions.hint: Do not rewrite history that others already have.
questions.explain: `git revert` makes a new commit that undoes the old one, so history stays the same for your teammates. A hard reset plus force-push rewrites shared history and can break their work.

questions.prompt: Type the full Git command (starting with `git`) that shows your list of saved stashes.
questions.hint: Three words: the tool, the feature, and what you want to see.
questions.explain: `git stash list` shows entries like `stash@{0}: WIP on main`, newest first.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of ESLint?
choices: Finding likely bugs and problems in your code
Uploading your code to GitHub after each commit
Installing any npm packages that are missing
Making your code run faster in the browser
questions.hint: It reads your code and warns you.
questions.explain: ESLint reads your code and warns about problems, like unused variables or names that were never defined. It does not upload code or install packages.

questions.prompt: What does this command do?
choices: Checks the code for logic bugs and stops at the first error
Deletes files that are badly formatted
Reformats the files in the project to a consistent style
Writes a new `package.json` file
questions.hint: Prettier makes code look pretty.
questions.explain: Prettier is a formatter. `--write` rewrites files with consistent spacing, quotes, and line breaks, so the team stops arguing about style.

questions.prompt: ESLint and Prettier can be used together in the same project.
questions.hint: They do different jobs.
questions.explain: Many projects use both: Prettier handles formatting, and ESLint catches code problems.

questions.prompt: Complete the command so ESLint also repairs the problems it can fix by itself: `npx eslint . ____`. Type only the missing option.
questions.hint: It is one short word after two dashes.
questions.explain: `--fix` tells ESLint to repair simple problems in your files, such as using `const` for a variable that never changes. Problems it cannot fix safely are still listed for you.

questions.prompt: Why is `eslint` in `devDependencies` here?
choices: It is too big to go in the normal `dependencies` list
It is used while you develop, not when the app runs
It runs only on the production server, not locally
npm sorts packages there by the first letter of the name
questions.hint: Does the user's browser ever run the linter?
questions.explain: `devDependencies` are tools for building, testing, and linting. `dependencies` are packages the app needs to run, like `react`.

questions.prompt: Where does `npm install -D prettier` record the package?
choices: Under `devDependencies` in `package.json`
In a global folder outside the project, for all projects
Only in `node_modules`, nowhere else
Under `dependencies` in `package.json`
questions.hint: The `-D` is short for a longer option.
questions.explain: `-D` is short for `--save-dev`. It adds the package to `devDependencies`.

questions.prompt: Which statements about `package-lock.json` are true? Select all that apply.
choices: npm updates it when you install or remove packages
It should be listed in `.gitignore`
You edit it by hand to add new packages
You should commit it to Git
questions.hint: Think about who creates the file, and who else needs it.
questions.explain: npm creates and updates the lockfile for you. Commit it so everyone installs the same versions. Use `npm install` to add packages instead of editing it.

questions.prompt: Your app reads an API key from a `.env` file. What should you commit to Git?
choices: A screenshot of the `.env` file in your docs folder
The key pasted into a comment in your code instead
A `.env.example` with names but no real values
The `.env` file itself, so teammates already have the key
questions.hint: Share the shape, not the secret.
questions.explain: Keep `.env` in `.gitignore`. A `.env.example` shows which variables are needed, and each person fills in their own values.

questions.prompt: What is `package-lock.json` for?
choices: It stops other people from editing your `package.json`
It records exact versions so every install is the same
It stores your npm login token so you stay signed in
It lists the scripts you can run with `npm run`
questions.hint: Think "same install on every machine".
questions.explain: The lockfile pins exact versions of every package, including nested ones. Commit it so your team and CI install the same thing.

questions.prompt: Why do projects put `node_modules/` in `.gitignore`?
choices: It is large and can be recreated with `npm install`
Git cannot store JavaScript files that other people wrote
It holds your passwords and npm login details
npm deletes and rebuilds it every time you commit
questions.hint: Everything in it comes from `package.json` and the lockfile.
questions.explain: `node_modules` can hold thousands of files. Since `npm install` rebuilds it from `package.json` and the lockfile, there is no need to commit it.

questions.prompt: In `package.json`, what versions does `"lodash": "^4.17.21"` allow?
choices: Any version from 4.17.21 up, including 5.x and later
Only exactly 4.17.21
Only 4.17.x patch versions
Any 4.x version from 4.17.21 up, but not 5.0.0
questions.hint: The caret allows updates that should not break your code.
questions.explain: The caret `^` allows minor and patch updates but not a new major version. Major versions can contain breaking changes.

questions.prompt: What is special about `npm ci` compared with `npm install`?
choices: It updates every package to the newest version it can find
It installs packages only for the current user account
It installs the exact lockfile versions and nothing else
It checks your code for style errors before installing
questions.hint: It is popular in automated builds.
questions.explain: `npm ci` does a clean install: it removes `node_modules` and installs exact lockfile versions. It never changes `package.json` or the lockfile, which makes builds reliable.

questions.prompt: For a web server app, which packages would usually go in `devDependencies`? Select all that apply.
choices: `eslint`
`prettier`
`vitest`
`express`
questions.hint: Which one does the app need while it is running?
questions.explain: Linters, formatters, and test runners are only used during development. `express` runs in production, so it belongs in `dependencies`.

questions.prompt: In Node.js, how do you read an environment variable named `API_KEY`?
choices: `window.API_KEY`
`process.env.API_KEY`
`env.get("API_KEY")`
`require("API_KEY")`
questions.hint: Browsers have `window`; Node has a different global object for the running program.
questions.explain: Node puts environment variables on `process.env`. Values are always strings or `undefined` if not set.

questions.prompt: If you push an API key by accident, deleting it in a new commit is enough to make it safe.
questions.hint: What is still in the history?
questions.explain: The key stays in the old commit, and others may have copied it. Revoke or rotate the key right away, then remove it from the code.

questions.prompt: Which file name is commonly used for local environment variables that must not be committed? Type the file name, including the leading dot.
questions.hint: It is a hidden file with three letters after the dot.
questions.explain: A `.env` file holds local settings and secrets. Add it to `.gitignore` so it never reaches the repository.
